Choking in a baby (under 1 year): If the baby can’t cough, cry or breathe, or is turning blue, start at once and have someone call 112.
If the baby is coughing and crying, let them cough and stay with them.
If they can’t cough: lay the baby face down along your forearm with the head lower than the body; support the jaw with your hand.
Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
If the object hasn’t come out, turn the baby onto their back and give 5 firm chest thrusts with two fingers in the middle of the chest, just below the nipple line.
Keep alternating 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until the object comes out.
If the baby becomes unconscious, call 112, put the phone on speaker and start basic life support.
Don’t hold the baby upside down by the feet and shake them.
Don’t try to remove an object you can’t see with your finger.
Choking in a child (over 1 year)
If the child can’t speak, cough or breathe, start at once and have someone call 112.
If they can cough, encourage them to keep coughing.
If they can’t cough: lean the child forward and give 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.

If it hasn’t come out, stand behind them and put your arms around their waist; place a fist just above the belly button, grasp it with your other hand and pull sharply inwards and upwards 5 times (Heimlich).
Keep alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out.
If they become unconscious, call 112 and start basic life support.
If abdominal thrusts were used, the child must be seen by a doctor.
Basic life support (baby and child)
If the child is unresponsive and not breathing normally: call 112, put the phone on speaker and follow the call handler’s instructions.
Call out and tap their shoulder; if there’s no response, shout for help and call 112.
Open the airway by gently tilting the head back and lifting the chin (keep a baby’s head in a neutral position); check breathing for 10 seconds.
If they aren’t breathing normally, give 5 rescue breaths: over a baby’s mouth and nose together; for a child, pinch the nose and seal over the mouth.
Start chest compressions on the lower half of the breastbone at 100–120 a minute: about 4 cm with two fingers for a baby, about 5 cm with one or two hands for a child.
Continue with 15 compressions to 2 breaths. If you haven’t been trained, you can do compressions only, as the 112 call handler tells you.
Don’t stop until help arrives or the child starts breathing normally.
Febrile seizure (fit)
Call 112 if the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, it’s the first one, the child doesn’t wake up afterwards or has trouble breathing.
Stay calm and note the time.
Lay the child on their side somewhere safe; put something soft under the head.
Move hard and sharp objects away and loosen tight clothing.
When the seizure ends, keep them in the recovery position and watch their breathing.
Take a child who has had a first febrile seizure to a doctor even if it has stopped.
Don’t put a finger, spoon or anything else in their mouth.
Don’t try to stop their movements by force.
Don’t put them in cold water or wipe them with alcohol.
Poisoning (medicines, cleaning products, plants)
If the child is unconscious, having a seizure or struggling to breathe, call 112. Otherwise call 114 National Poison Information Centre straight away.
Take away anything left in the child’s hands and mouth, and rinse their mouth with water.
Keep the product’s box or bottle with you; you should be able to say its name, the amount and the time.
Call 114 and follow the instructions.
If it got on the skin or in the eyes, rinse with plenty of running water for 15 minutes.
Don’t try to make them vomit.
Don’t give milk, yogurt or anything else to drink (unless 114 tells you to).
Burns and scalds
Go to A&E or call 112 if the burn is larger than the baby’s palm; on the face, hands, feet, joints or genitals; blistered, white or charred; or electrical or chemical.
Immediately hold the burned area under cool (not ice-cold) running water for 20 minutes.
Remove clothing and jewellery if not stuck; don’t pull off clothing that’s stuck.
Make sure the child doesn’t get cold.
Cover the burn loosely with clean cling film or a clean non-stick cloth.
Don’t apply ice, toothpaste, yogurt, oil or tomato paste.
Don’t burst blisters.
Head bump / fall

Call 112 if there is loss of consciousness, a seizure, vomiting more than once, unusual drowsiness, unsteadiness, or blood or fluid from the ears or nose. For a baby under 1 with a noticeable swelling, see a doctor.
Calm the child and apply something cold wrapped in a cloth to the bumped area.
Watch closely for the next 24 hours; they can sleep, but check that they wake every few hours.
See a doctor if their behaviour changes in an unusual way.
Nosebleed
Go to A&E if it doesn’t stop within 20 minutes, is very heavy or followed a hard blow.
Sit the child down and tilt their head slightly forward.
Pinch the soft part of the nose with two fingers for 10 minutes without letting go; they should breathe through the mouth.
Once it stops, tell them not to blow their nose for a few hours.
Don’t tilt the head back (blood gets swallowed).
Don’t plug the nose with cotton wool.
